title: Sudden Pain at the Sink

patient.name: Mr Rajan s/o Muthusamy
patient.presenting_complaint: Red, painful eyes for 2 days with blurred vision, starting after shampooing his hair

history.hpc: Mr Rajan presents to the Acute Care clinic with red eyes for 2 days. He says 'Suddenly very pain after I shampoo my hair, the pain like 8 out of 10.' His vision became blurred after shampooing of the eyes; he tries to blink but the vision stays blur. He does not remember anything hitting his eye. He has not seen any doctor and has not taken any medicine. Today he also has watery eyes, a headache, nausea and vomiting, and says he is unable to see the light.
history.pmhx: Seen an eye doctor only once, in 2023, for dry eyes. Does not wear contact lenses.
history.social_hx: Works in a warehouse. No contact lens use.

investigations.history_structure: Take a structured history: presenting complaint, history of presenting complaint (onset, trigger, pain score, vision, discharge), associated/systemic symptoms, past ocular history, contact lens use, medications, allergies and family history
investigations.red_flags: Possible chemical/irritant exposure to the eyes (shampoo) with sudden severe pain and blurred vision; severe pain with headache, nausea and vomiting and inability to tolerate light are additional red flags
investigations.triage_action: This is not a routine red eye — recognise the urgency and escalate immediately for irrigation/assessment rather than routine queueing

diagnosis: A thorough, structured history identifies a sudden, severe, painful red eye with blurred vision following shampooing, raising concern about chemical/irritant exposure to the eyes, with additional red flags of severe pain, headache, nausea, vomiting and photophobia. The OA recognises this as a potential ocular emergency requiring urgent escalation (immediate irrigation if chemical exposure is suspected, and urgent doctor assessment), and does not attempt to diagnose or treat independently.

immediate: Introduce yourself, confirm patient identity and take the history in a calm, systematic way
Elicit the history of presenting complaint: onset, the shampooing trigger, pain score, change in vision, discharge and watering
Specifically ask about chemical/irritant getting into the eyes and any first aid (rinsing) already done
Ask about associated and systemic symptoms: headache, nausea, vomiting, light sensitivity
Take past ocular history (previous dry eyes, no contact lens use), medications, allergies and family history
Recognise the red flags and escalate urgently — if chemical exposure is suspected, irrigation should not be delayed
Document the history accurately and hand over clearly to the nurse/doctor
follow_up: Urgent doctor assessment with formal visual acuity, pH check and slit lamp examination
Commence copious irrigation immediately if a chemical/irritant exposure is confirmed or suspected
Ensure the patient is not left waiting in a routine queue given the red-flag presentation
patient_education: Reassure the distressed patient and explain that he will be seen urgently
Explain why any chemical in the eye needs immediate rinsing and assessment
Advise him not to rub the eyes and to report any worsening pain or vision while waiting
